section_summary: This section traces U.S. diplomatic, consular, military-intelligence, and export-control reporting on Japanese aviation from 1932 through 1939. It covers Japanese air operations at Shanghai and in China, proposed or actual transfers of American and European aircraft and technology, aviation-related materials and factories, prospective air bases, and Japanese aircraft performance. Much of the section consists of cross-reference sheets directing readers to documents filed elsewhere, alongside correspondence over the Glenn L. Martin BM-2 bomber, Mitsubishi engine parts, the Flying Flea, and a reported Japanese light-metal plant.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on Japanese flights over the Shanghai Settlement
subfiles.about: Records a telegram concerning Japanese aircraft flying over the Shanghai International Settlement.
subfiles.summary: The sheet refers the reader to telegram no. 78 of February 19, 1932, filed under another decimal number. It notes that Japanese practice flights over the Settlement would be discontinued unless considered absolutely necessary.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 78 on flights over the Shanghai Settlement
subfiles.about: Reports Japan's qualified promise to stop military aircraft from flying over the Shanghai Settlement.
subfiles.summary: The Senior Consul received a Japanese reply stating that aviators had been instructed not to fly over the Settlement. The reply retained an exception for flights deemed indispensable to the Settlement's defense or to the protection of Japanese lives and property, making it less satisfactory than an earlier oral assurance to Admiral Taylor.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on accidental Japanese bombing in the Settlement
subfiles.about: Indexes a report that Japanese bombing in the Settlement resulted from defective bomb racks.
subfiles.summary: The note refers to Shanghai telegram no. 76, filed under another decimal classification. It summarizes the Japanese explanation that the bombing was accidental and occurred without the aviators' knowledge because of defective bomb racks.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 76 on Japanese firing and bombing in Shanghai
subfiles.about: Transmits Japan's explanation and apology for machine-gun fire and accidental bomb release in the Settlement.
subfiles.summary: Japanese naval headquarters claimed that aviators fired their machine guns because they mistakenly believed the location lay outside the American defense area. It attributed the falling bombs to a defective aircraft bomb rack and expressed regret, while promising strict precautions against future danger to life and property.

subfiles.title: Note on Dutch East Indies bauxite for Japanese aircraft production
subfiles.about: Reports a Japanese agreement to obtain bauxite from Bintan Island for aluminum and aircraft production.
subfiles.summary: A Japanese company operating aluminum works in Formosa reportedly agreed to take 24,000 tons of bauxite annually from the Nibam Company in the Dutch East Indies. The bauxite deposits were on Bintan Island near Singapore, and the material was said to be needed for building Japan's air fleet.

subfiles.title: Confidential note on alleged physiological limitations of Japanese aviators
subfiles.about: Indexes an allegation that anatomical differences supposedly prevented Japanese pilots from attaining the highest ability.
subfiles.summary: The note cross-references a confidential report filed under another decimal number. It records a now-discredited racialized assertion that a supposed defect in Japanese ear canals impaired equilibrium and made elite aviation performance physically impossible.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on possible German aviation aid to Japan
subfiles.about: Indexes a despatch concerning possible German aircraft materials or instructors for Japan.
subfiles.summary: The note records the possibility of an agreement under which Germany would supply Japan with aircraft materials or instructors. It adds that German aircraft factories and pilots were already heavily occupied with the development of Germany's own air resources.

subfiles.title: Note on proposed Japanese manufacture of Triangle parachutes
subfiles.about: Records departmental approval for foreign sale and manufacture of Triangle Parachute Equipment and Japanese interest in production rights.
subfiles.summary: The War and Navy Departments reportedly had no objection to foreign sale and manufacture of Triangle parachute equipment. After Mikuni Shoten created Japanese interest in the product, Mitsubishi Shoji Kaisha sought a proposal for manufacturing rights within the Japanese Empire.

subfiles.title: Note on export of Lear-O-Scope direction finders
subfiles.about: Indexes a request to ship Lear-O-Scope radio direction finders to Japan and Mexico.
subfiles.summary: Charles H. Payne requested government permission to export the Lear-O-Scope radio direction finder. The intended destinations were Japan and Mexico.

subfiles.title: Glenn L. Martin request concerning sale of BM-2 bomber designs
subfiles.from: J. T. Hartson, Glenn L. Martin Company
subfiles.about: Requests a government policy ruling on selling BM-2 dive-bomber design data and a manufacturing license to Japanese representatives.
subfiles.summary: The company had been approached by Japanese representatives seeking drawings and manufacturing rights for the BM-2 Dive Bomber formerly built for the U.S. Navy. Hartson argued that the Navy no longer appeared interested in the model and that proceeds from the sale would strengthen the company, but he sought a formal government statement before proceeding.

subfiles.title: Referral of the BM-2 proposal to the Secretary of the Navy
subfiles.from: R. Walton Moore, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Claude A. Swanson, Secretary of the Navy
subfiles.about: Asks the Navy what reply should be given to Glenn L. Martin's proposed sale of BM-2 designs to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Moore enclosed the company's September 20 request concerning Japanese purchase of the bomber's design data and manufacturing license. He asked the Secretary of the Navy to indicate the appropriate response.

subfiles.title: Interim reply to the Glenn L. Martin Company
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the BM-2 request and advises that it has been referred to the Navy.
subfiles.summary: The State Department acknowledged the company's September 20 letter about selling BM-2 design data and manufacturing rights. Green stated that the question had been sent to the Secretary of the Navy and that a further reply would follow.

subfiles.title: Glenn L. Martin request for expedited BM-2 decision
subfiles.from: J. T. Hartson, Glenn L. Martin Company
subfiles.about: Requests prompt action because a Japanese purchasing party was expected to visit on October 11.
subfiles.summary: Hartson followed up on the company's request to sell BM-2 design data and a manufacturing license. He asked for an early decision after learning that an interested Japanese party intended to visit the company on October 11.

subfiles.title: Second interim reply on the BM-2 proposal
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Advises that the Navy had not yet decided whether the BM-2 contained secret military equipment.
subfiles.summary: Green acknowledged the company's follow-up letter of September 30. He explained that the Secretary of the Navy had not yet reported whether the BM-2 incorporated equipment regarded as a military secret and promised to communicate once an answer arrived.

subfiles.title: Navy objection to releasing BM-2 designs to Japan
subfiles.about: Reports War and Navy Department opposition to selling BM-2 design data and manufacturing rights to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Navy returned the Glenn L. Martin request for release of the BM-2 material. Both the War and Navy Departments objected because disclosure would prejudice the safeguarding of military secrets and the interests of national defense.

subfiles.title: Copy of State Department referral to the Navy
subfiles.from: R. Walton Moore, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Claude A. Swanson, Secretary of the Navy
subfiles.about: Reproduces the State Department's request for Navy guidance on the BM-2 sale proposal.
subfiles.summary: The copy restates that Japanese representatives wished to buy design data and a manufacturing license for the BM-2. Moore asked the Navy to advise what answer should be sent to the Glenn L. Martin Company.

subfiles.title: Copy of Glenn L. Martin's BM-2 request
subfiles.from: J. T. Hartson, Glenn L. Martin Company
subfiles.about: Reproduces the company's case for permission to sell BM-2 drawings and manufacturing rights to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The company described Japanese interest in manufacturing the BM-2 or similar dive-bombing equipment. It argued that the aircraft had not been ordered since 1933, appeared to be of no further Navy interest, and represented an otherwise idle commercial asset.

subfiles.title: Final rejection of the BM-2 sale proposal
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Informs the company that the War and Navy Departments opposed release of the BM-2 material.
subfiles.summary: Green conveyed the Navy's response to the company's proposal. The government objected because releasing the design data and manufacturing license would endanger military secrets and conflict with national-defense interests.

subfiles.title: Notification to the Acting Secretary of War on the BM-2 decision
subfiles.from: R. Walton Moore, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Harry H. Woodring, Acting Secretary of War
subfiles.about: Provides the War Department with a copy of the rejection sent to the Glenn L. Martin Company.
subfiles.summary: Moore informed Woodring of the State Department's response to the Japanese BM-2 proposal. A copy of the letter sent to the company was enclosed for the War Department's information.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment to the Secretary of the Navy on the BM-2 decision
subfiles.from: R. Walton Moore, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Claude A. Swanson, Secretary of the Navy
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the Navy's objection and encloses the State Department's reply to Glenn L. Martin.
subfiles.summary: Moore acknowledged receipt of the Navy's October 29 decision concerning the proposed Japanese purchase. He enclosed a copy of the rejection sent to the Glenn L. Martin Company.

subfiles.title: Mitsubishi inquiry about export licenses for aircraft-engine parts
subfiles.from: Mitsubishi Shoji Kaisha, Ltd., New York
subfiles.about: Asks whether licenses were required for two imminent shipments of aircraft-engine parts and requests additional application forms.
subfiles.summary: Mitsubishi reported planned departures from New York and San Francisco on November 29 and 30 and enclosed license applications in case they were required. Customs personnel believed no licenses were necessary, but the company sought an authoritative answer because the regulations did not expressly discuss parts or accessories; it also requested blank forms and updated printed regulations.

subfiles.title: State Department reply on aircraft-engine-part licenses
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Advises Mitsubishi that no license was required to export aircraft-engine parts to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The State Department cited its arms-trafficking regulations and stated that aircraft-engine parts did not require an export license. Mitsubishi's two applications were therefore rejected and returned, while twenty blank application forms were supplied as requested.

subfiles.title: Despatch on midget airplanes in Japan
subfiles.from: Richard F. Boyce, American Consul, Yokohama
subfiles.about: Reports on Japanese manufacture, importation, military use, and subsidization of Flying Flea light aircraft.
subfiles.summary: Boyce described reports concerning a factory for the French-designed Pou du Ciel or Flying Flea and relayed an aviator's claim that forty imported examples were already in Japanese service. The Japanese Army had reportedly designated the low-powered single-seater as a preliminary trainer, and purchasers of domestically manufactured examples were said to qualify for a ¥1,000 subsidy.

subfiles.title: Japan Advertiser excerpt on the Flying Flea subsidy
subfiles.about: Reports a ¥1,000 subsidy for purchasers of low-powered airplanes manufactured in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Imperial Aeronautical Society reportedly approved a subsidy for Japanese-made aircraft with engines of no more than fifty horsepower. The measure chiefly applied to the Lark or Flying Flea, reducing its effective price to about ¥2,600, while a third-class pilot's license required only ten hours of solo flying.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on expansion of Japanese naval aviation
subfiles.about: Indexes a report on planned increases in aircraft carriers, auxiliary vessels, and the Japanese naval air force.
subfiles.summary: The note refers to despatch no. 1953, filed under another decimal classification. It summarizes a naval program for the coming fiscal year that included more aircraft carriers and auxiliaries and an enlarged naval air force.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on rumored German-Italian aviation aid to Japan
subfiles.about: Indexes a telegram about rumors of secret German and Italian technical and material assistance to Japanese aviation.
subfiles.summary: The note concerns the rumored German-Japanese agreement then under discussion in Tokyo. It records claims that a secret provision would supply Japan with German and Italian technical and material aid, particularly for aviation.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 235 on the German-Japanese agreement
subfiles.about: Reports diplomatic information and rumors concerning the German-Japanese agreement and possible aviation assistance.
subfiles.summary: The Finnish minister found that neither the Japanese Foreign Office nor the German Embassy denied negotiations, although both denied that a formal international agreement was involved. Rumors held that Italy joined an anti-communist front, Poland had declined participation, and a secret arrangement would provide German and Italian aviation assistance enabling Japan to shorten its army-replenishment program. The Belgian Embassy also reported that the Privy Council was considering the agreement.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on Pratas Reef and Japanese air-base plans
subfiles.about: Indexes a London telegram about Japanese occupation of Pratas Reef and possible air-base construction.
subfiles.summary: The note summarizes British and French concern over the occupation of Pratas Reef, dismantling of its meteorological station, and reported plans for an airplane base. It also records a proposed joint demarche in Tokyo and British interest in possible U.S. action.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 593 on Japanese island occupations and air bases
subfiles.about: Reports British and French concern over Japanese moves at Pratas, Hainan, and the Paracels and asks what action the United States contemplated.
subfiles.summary: The British Foreign Office reported that Japan had occupied Pratas Reef, dismantled its valuable weather station, and intended to establish an air base; it also possessed secret information about a planned attack on Hainan. Britain and France feared possible occupation of the disputed Paracels and instructed their ambassadors in Tokyo to make a joint demarche. British officials stressed the resulting danger to sea communications from Singapore and hoped the United States might make similar representations.

subfiles.title: Handwritten abstract on Japanese pursuit aircraft over Shiuchow
subfiles.about: Summarizes reports of unusually capable Japanese pursuit aircraft raiding the Shiuchow airplane factory.
subfiles.summary: The note identifies Japanese pursuit planes secretly participating in raids on an aircraft factory in Guangdong. It highlights their reportedly remarkable climb, speed, and maneuverability and notes that the factory had completed a run of aircraft.

subfiles.title: Despatch on the performance of Japanese pursuit planes
subfiles.from: Addison E. Southard, American Consul General, Hong Kong
subfiles.about: Relays Charles Healy Day's eyewitness account of advanced Japanese fighters attacking the Shiuchow Aircraft Works.
subfiles.summary: Day reported that Japanese low-wing monoplanes with retractable landing gear decisively outperformed Chinese Hawk II and Hawk III fighters in speed, climb, and maneuverability during raids on the factory. He estimated speeds above 280 miles per hour and climbs exceeding 3,000 feet per minute, described their radial engines and auxiliary fuel arrangements, and said Chinese losses were severe. Southard added that continued raids might force the factory to relocate northward toward Hankou.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on Italian airplanes and pilots sent to Japan
subfiles.about: Indexes a despatch transmitting a military attaché report on Italian aircraft and pilots sent to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The note refers to despatch no. 862 under a different decimal classification. Its subject is the shipment of Italian airplanes to Japan and the dispatch of Italian pilots there.

subfiles.title: Ithaca reader's inquiry about American aircraft exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Asks the Department to explain a newspaper image of American warplanes being shipped to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Knott enclosed a clipping about aircraft exports so that she could explain the issue to her eleven-year-old son. Her note expresses distress about the arms trade and asks where such activity would lead.

subfiles.title: Ithaca Journal clipping: America Sends War Planes to Japan
subfiles.about: Shows an American fighting aircraft being loaded at Los Angeles for shipment to Japan and criticizes continuing trade during the war in China.
subfiles.summary: The caption describes American-made planes as a common export to Japan while diplomats debated the undeclared war and application of U.S. neutrality law. It also cites Senator Nye's assertion that the bombs which sank the Panay on the Yangtze were probably American-made.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on alleged Seversky aircraft production for Japan
subfiles.about: Indexes informant information that Seversky planned to manufacture and ship twenty advanced aircraft to Japan.
subfiles.summary: A Justice Department informant alleged that the Seversky Airplane Company at Farmingdale, Long Island, was building twenty large aircraft for shipment to Japan. The planes were said to outperform U.S. fighting aircraft.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on restricting aircraft sales to belligerents
subfiles.about: Suggests that voluntary restrictions on aircraft sales should apply to Germany and Italy as well as Japan.
subfiles.summary: Scott responded to the Secretary's suggestion that aircraft manufacturers refuse sales to governments bombing civilians. He recommended including Germany and Italy and forwarded a letter to Clark M. Eichelberger proposing revision of the Neutrality Act to prohibit such sales.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on Japanese aircraft purchases in the United States
subfiles.about: Indexes a telegram reporting export licenses for fourteen aircraft and prospective Japanese purchases of many more bombers.
subfiles.summary: The note states that licenses for fourteen planes were issued on June 9. It also reports that Japanese interests had approached an American company about immediately buying a large number of bombers and anticipated further major purchases.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on Heinkel bombers shipped to Japan
subfiles.about: Indexes a report that four Heinkel He 111 bombers were observed aboard a Japanese steamer bound for Japan.
subfiles.summary: An American Army officer reportedly observed four Heinkel 111 bombers on a Japanese vessel. The aircraft were being transported from Germany to Japan.

subfiles.title: Departmental routing note concerning the Austrian magnesium report
subfiles.about: Asks whether the report on an aviation-related Japanese light-metal plant should be sent to naval intelligence.
subfiles.summary: The fragmentary handwritten note routes the attached information within the State Department. It appears to ask whether the material would be worth forwarding to the Office of Naval Intelligence.

subfiles.title: Letter on a reported Japanese light-metal plant
subfiles.from: Eliot B. Coulter, American Consul General, Beirut
subfiles.about: Transmits Ernst Gutman's information that an Austrian magnesium firm helped establish a similar aviation-metal plant in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Gutman reported that Japanese technicians and army officers visited the firm's Radenthein plant after its anti-Nazi managing director, Konrad Erdmann, had been removed. He alleged that the firm then cooperated, without its American president Emil Winter's knowledge, in establishing a Japanese plant. The product of concern was a light metal considered particularly valuable for aircraft construction, and Coulter regarded Gutman as a credible source.

subfiles.title: Reply to the American Consul General at Beirut
subfiles.to: Eliot B. Coulter, American Consul General, Beirut
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the report on the Japanese light-metal plant and states that it was forwarded to the War and Navy Departments.
subfiles.summary: Murray thanked the consul general for the February 21 information supplied by the former Austrian consul in Damascus. He stated that the report had been sent to the appropriate authorities in both military departments.

subfiles.title: Transmission of Japanese light-metal report to the Navy
subfiles.about: Forwards excerpts from the Beirut report to the Office of Naval Intelligence.
subfiles.summary: The State Department transmitted excerpts concerning reported plans to establish a Japanese plant producing light metal for aircraft construction. Because only one set of the booklet and map existed, those enclosures went to the War Department while the Navy received the textual excerpts.

subfiles.title: Transmission of Japanese light-metal report to the War Department
subfiles.about: Forwards the Beirut report, booklet, and maps to the Military Intelligence Division.
subfiles.summary: The State Department sent the War Department excerpts concerning the planned Japanese light-metal plant together with the sole available copies of the associated booklet and maps. It advised that the Navy Department was receiving the excerpts but not the original enclosures.
